problems.title: Catapult launch and wind over deck
problems.setup: A carrier strike fighter launches at W = 200 kN with S = 40 m² and C_Lmax = 1.8 in launch configuration. It must leave the catapult at an airspeed of at least 1.1V_stall. The ship steams into the wind giving wind over deck WOD = 15 m/s. The catapult stroke is 90 m. Sea level: ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: Find the 1g stall speed in launch configuration.
Find the catapult end speed relative to the deck.
sol: Airspeed = deck speed + WOD, so V_end = 1.1V_stall − WOD

parts.ask: Find the mean acceleration along the 90 m stroke, in g.
sol: Constant acceleration from rest: a = V_end²/(2s)

parts.ask: The wind dies and WOD drops to 5 m/s. The catapult end speed stays at the value from part 2. What is the heaviest aircraft it can launch?
sol: Required airspeed scales with V_stall ∝ √W, so W ∝ V²

parts.ask: On the launch bulletin plot of minimum end speed versus launch weight, what shape is the required curve?
parts.a: V_end = 1.1√(2W/(ρSC_Lmax)) − WOD: a √W curve shifted down by the wind over deck
w: A straight line V_end ∝ W, shifted up by the wind over deck
A √W curve shifted up by the wind over deck
A curve V_end ∝ W², independent of wind over deck
sol: Required airspeed grows as √W from the lift equation
Wind over deck supplies part of that airspeed, so the deck relative curve moves down by WOD

problems.x: Wind over deck supplies airspeed for free, and because launch weight scales with airspeed squared, a few m/s of wind buys a large weight margin.

problems.title: Human powered aircraft power budget
problems.setup: A human powered aircraft (pilot included) weighs W = 1000 N, with S = 30 m², span b = 30 m, Oswald efficiency e = 0.95 and C_D0 = 0.015, so C_D = C_D0 + KC_L² with K = 1/(πeAR). The wing has C_Lmax = 1.2. Propeller efficiency η_p = 0.85. Fly at low altitude, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, and neglect ground effect. A fit pilot can sustain about 250 W of shaft power for an hour.

parts.ask: Find the lift coefficient for minimum power required from the polar.
sol: Minimum power: C_D0 = KC_L²/3, so C_L = √(3C_D0/K)

parts.ask: Compare that C_L with C_Lmax = 1.2. What should the pilot do?
parts.a: The minimum power point lies beyond stall, so fly at the highest safe C_L, a little below C_Lmax
w: Fly at the polar optimum C_L, since the polar sets the operating point
Fly at the minimum drag C_L = √(C_D0/K) instead
Fly at C_L ≈ 0.6, since minimum power always sits well above stall speed
sol: The polar optimum assumes C_L is free; here the stall constraint is active
Power falls as C_L rises toward the optimum, so the best feasible choice sits just below C_Lmax with a stall margin

parts.ask: At C_L = 1.1, find the pilot shaft power required.
sol: P_R = DV = 182 W; shaft P = P_R/η_p = 215 W, inside the 250 W budget

parts.ask: Keep S = 30 m² and C_L = 1.1 but stretch the span to 36 m. Find the new shaft power.

problems.x: Human powered aircraft fly slowly near C_Lmax, where induced drag is a large share of the total, so added span cuts the pilot's power directly.

problems.title: The same drone on Earth and Titan
problems.setup: A 10 kg fixed wing drone has S = 1 m², C_Lmax = 1.6 and polar C_D = 0.03 + 0.05C_L². Earth sea level: g = 9.81 m/s², ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Titan surface: g = 1.35 m/s², ρ = 5.3 kg/m³ (cold, dense nitrogen). Same airframe and mass on both worlds.

parts.ask: Find the stall speed on Earth.
Find the stall speed on Titan.
Find the minimum power required on Earth.
Find the minimum power required on Titan.
sol: Same C_L and C_D, so P_min ∝ W·√(W/ρ) = W^(3/2)/√ρ

parts.ask: A rotorcraft on Titan hovers using ideal momentum theory. How does its hover power ratio, Titan over Earth, compare with the fixed wing ratio above?
parts.a: It is the same ratio, since hover power P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA) also scales as W^(3/2)/√ρ
w: It is the square root of the fixed wing ratio, since hover power scales as W/√ρ
It equals the weight ratio 1.35/9.81, since hover thrust equals weight
It is the inverse of the fixed wing ratio, since rotors work best in thin air
sol: Hover: P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA) with T = W
Fixed wing at a fixed C_L: P ∝ W^(3/2)/√ρ

problems.x: Power to stay aloft scales as W^(3/2)/√ρ for wings and rotors alike, so Titan's low gravity and dense air cut it by a factor of about 40.

problems.title: Climbing and accelerating segment
problems.setup: A fighter must climb at dh/dt = 50 m/s while accelerating at dV/dt = 3 m/s², passing V = 200 m/s at 5000 m (ISA ρ = 0.736 kg/m³), wings level (n = 1). Polar C_D = 0.02 + 0.1C_L². W_TO/S = 4000 Pa, weight fraction β = 0.9, thrust lapse α = 0.7. Take g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: From the energy equation, find the specific excess power P_s the segment demands.
sol: Energy height h_e = h + V²/(2g), so P_s = dh_e/dt = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt

parts.ask: Find T_SL/W_TO from the master equation.
Which bracket term is largest?
sol: Dividing P_s by V turns (V/g)dV/dt into (1/g)dV/dt, which is the largest here

parts.ask: Same climb rate at constant speed (dV/dt = 0). Find T_SL/W_TO.

problems.x: The master equation is the energy equation divided by βW and V: each term is a drag, climb or acceleration demand on thrust loading, scaled by β/α back to sea level takeoff.

problems.title: Maneuver envelope at altitude and light weight
problems.setup: An aerobatic trainer has W/S = 3000 Pa at design weight, C_Lmax = 1.5 and positive limit load factor n_max = 6. Sea level ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³; at 6000 m (ISA) ρ = 0.660 kg/m³. Equivalent airspeed V_e = V√(ρ/ρ₀).

parts.ask: Find the 1g stall speed in EAS.
Find the corner (maneuver) speed V_A in EAS.
sol: Stall curve n = (V/V_S)² meets n_max at V_A = V_S√n_max

parts.ask: Find V_A as a true airspeed at 6000 m.
sol: In EAS the envelope is the same at every altitude

parts.ask: Where is the maneuver diagram aerodynamically limited?
parts.a: Along the stall curve n = (V/V_S)² from V_S up to V_A, where C_Lmax caps the load factor
w: Along the n_max line from V_A to V_D, where the wing reaches C_Lmax
At V_D, where the dive speed caps the load factor
Along the gust lines, which set the lift limit at every speed
sol: Left of V_A the wing stalls before reaching n_max: lift limit
Right of V_A the n_max line is a structural limit, and V_D is a speed limit

parts.ask: After fuel burn the weight is 80% of design weight, with n_max still 6. Find the new V_A in EAS.
sol: V_S ∝ √(W/S), so V_A ∝ √W at fixed n_max

problems.x: Drawn in equivalent airspeed the V-n envelope holds at every altitude, and the stall speed and corner speed both scale with √W as weight changes.

problems.title: Same thrust, more air: why bypass pays
problems.setup: An engine must give T = 48 kN at flight speed V₀ = 240 m/s. Option A is a turbojet with mass flow 80 kg/s. Option B adds a fan with bypass ratio 5 on the same 80 kg/s core, so 480 kg/s in total. Treat each option as one uniform exhaust stream at ambient pressure, fuel mass neglected: T = ṁ(V_e − V₀).

parts.ask: Find the propulsive efficiency of option A.
Find the propulsive efficiency of option B.
Find the ratio of kinetic energy power left in the wake, option A over option B.
sol: Wasted power = ½ṁΔV²: A = ½·80·600² = 14.4 MW
Ratio = 6, while useful power TV₀ = 11.52 MW for both

parts.ask: Which statement explains the gain?
parts.a: For fixed thrust ṁΔV, moving more mass with a smaller ΔV leaves less kinetic energy ½ṁΔV² in the wake
w: The fan raises the core turbine inlet temperature, which raises thermal efficiency
A larger ΔV gives more thrust per kg of air, so the wake carries less energy
Bypass air adds thrust without adding any ram drag ṁV₀
sol: η_p is useful power over useful plus wasted wake power
Wasted power scales as T·ΔV/2, so smaller ΔV at the same T wins

parts.ask: Flight speed rises toward option B's exhaust velocity of about 340 m/s. What happens to its thrust, and what does this mean for fast aircraft?
parts.a: Thrust is ṁ(V_e − V₀), so as V₀ climbs toward V_e the velocity excess and the thrust collapse while ram drag ṁV₀ grows. Fast aircraft therefore use low bypass, high jet velocity engines and accept lower propulsive efficiency.
sol: T = ṁ(V_e − V₀) shrinks as V₀ approaches V_e (thrust lapse with speed)
High speed needs a high specific thrust, which means low bypass ratio

problems.x: High bypass engines gain propulsive efficiency by accelerating a large mass flow by a small velocity increment, which suits the speed range where exhaust velocity stays well above flight speed.
